documents: Devin & Zhong (2022), Characterization of Viscous Dissipative Heating in the Earth's Mantle Caused by Surface Forces, G-Cubed 23, e2021GC010218 (published PDF, 19 pp.)

entry.evidence: However, these previous studies mainly estimated dissipative heating during specific processes, and did not explore systematically how loading period, loading wavelength, viscosity structure, and viscosity [...]

steps.action: Cite earlier estimates that glaciation-deglaciation dissipation over the last glacial cycle is about 0.03 TW, far below the 44 TW surface heat flow.
steps.quote: the dissipative heating from the glaciation-deglaciation process has been estimated to be approximately 0.03 TW over the cycle

steps.action: Pose the question of how loading period, wavelength and viscosity structure control dissipation and the energy exchange in a loaded viscoelastic mantle.
steps.quote: did not explore systematically how loading period, loading wavelength, viscosity structure, and viscosity [...]

steps.action: Derive from the momentum equation, via the virtual work principle, an energy balance: surface work equals elastic energy plus viscous dissipation.
steps.quote: can be used to establish a relationship among the work done at the surface, the energy lost as heat to dissipation

steps.action: Use the finite element code CitcomVE, developed in the authors' earlier work for glacial isostatic adjustment and volcanic loading, solved in nondimensional form.
steps.quote: CitcomVE was developed to model deformation of a viscoelastic solid for glacial isostatic adjustment and volcanic loading problems

steps.action: Design a grid of 345 cases: three viscosity structures (uniform, stiff lid, stiff lid plus weak upper mantle), five wavelengths and 23 periods.
steps.quote: We compute a total of 345 different models defined by three viscosity structures, five loading wavelengths, and 23 loading periods.

steps.action: Compute a representative case (VS1, T = 40 τM, λ = 1.25D): topography, displacement, energy fluxes and the spatial pattern of dissipation.
steps.quote: We first present the results of a single case that has a uniform viscosity

steps.action: Check that the numerical powers of work, elastic energy and dissipation sum to zero at all times, as the analytic energy balance requires.
steps.quote: To check that this is indeed occurring in our numerical results

steps.action: Vary the loading period and find that long periods convert nearly all work to heat, while short periods store it elastically.
steps.quote: For a short period (Figure 4c), the opposite is true; very little energy is dissipated as heat

steps.action: Compare dissipation across viscosity structures against expectation: VS1 and VS2 are identical; VS3 gives less dissipation at long periods and more at short periods.
steps.quote: For all periods, VS1 and VS2 are producing identical amounts of dissipation, as we would expect

steps.action: Map the spatial and depth distribution of dissipation for VS1 and VS3 across periods and wavelengths (Figures 6-8).
steps.quote: Figure 7 shows that the spatial distribution of dissipation for VS3 is dependent on both period and wavelength.

steps.action: Compare the concentration of dissipation in the weak upper mantle with Hanyk et al. (2005) and Steinke et al. (2020), and add the lower-mantle exception at long wavelength and long period.
steps.quote: [...] that the dissipation is concentrated in the weak upper mantle layer is similar to that in Hanyk et al. (2005)

steps.action: Compute time-averaged work and dissipation fluxes and the conversion efficiency against period for VS1 and VS3.
steps.quote: The system's efficiency in converting mechanical energy to heat is defined as the time-averaged energy flux for dissipation divided by that for work.

steps.action: Vary wavelength (1.25D, 5D, 10D) for VS1 and find that energy fluxes and efficiency are insensitive to it.
steps.quote: The energy fluxes for work and dissipation and the efficiency of the system are in general not very sensitive to wavelength

steps.action: State limiting regularities: in the elastic limit work flux scales as 1/T and dissipation flux is constant; in the viscous limit both fall with slope steeper than 1.
steps.quote: at the short period (elastic) limit, energy flux of the work done at the surface increases nearly linearly with decreasing period T

steps.action: Rescale the VS3 results to reference viscosities of 10^18 to 10^22 Pa s and estimate glacial-cycle dissipation of about 3 mW/m2 (100 kyr, Fennoscandian wavelength) and about 2 mW/m2 (North American wavelength).
steps.quote: the results for VS3 which most closely models the Earth's interior are rescaled for several reference viscosities

steps.action: Compare the glacial estimates with the 0.03 TW of Hanyk et al. and Huang et al., scaled by ice-sheet area, and find them broadly consistent.
steps.quote: their surface heat flux results are broadly consistent with ours

steps.action: Estimate dissipation for 40 kyr Early Pleistocene cycles (about 9 mW/m2) and for seasonal Amazon loading (insignificant).
steps.quote: If a glacial cycle period 40,000 years for the Early Pleistocene is used

steps.action: Derive an equivalent rock load for degree-2 lunar tides by equating the tidal potential with a surface mass anomaly potential, giving about 1 m, doubled to 2 m for core-mantle boundary forcing.
steps.quote: Equating the tidal potential in Equation 18 to the gravitational potential produced by a degree-2 and order-0 mass anomaly

steps.action: Estimate tidal dissipation as insignificant today and about 13-26 TW at 4 Ga, using the lunar distance of Qin et al. (2018) and a viscosity of 10^19 Pa s.
steps.quote: the total power of tidal dissipation for the early Earth's mantle may be ∼13 TW from degree 2

steps.action: Propose that heating concentrated in a weak shallow layer feeds back to weaken it further, possibly forming an asthenosphere and global shallow melting, as on Io.
steps.quote: This positive feedback process may be responsible for a weak asthenosphere and even global-scale melting such as that on Io

steps.action: Conclude that the energy balance always holds, that the partition depends strongly on period and viscosity structure, and that dissipation concentrates in weak upper mantle layers.
steps.quote: the partition of energy between dissipative and elastic terms is strongly dependent on the loading period

tree.answer: Viscous dissipative heating in a viscoelastic mantle under exogenic surface loading
No; computed in 2-D Maxwell viscoelastic finite element models
Characterize the controls (period, wavelength, viscosity) on energy partition and dissipation; scale the results to Earth
Conditions set in a numerical model over a parameter grid of 345 cases
Energy balance verified numerically; efficiency insensitive to wavelength; consistent with earlier glacial estimates
Regularities kept within the tested parameter range; Earth estimates given as order-of-magnitude scalings

end.claim: Surface work on a Maxwell viscoelastic mantle is always balanced by elastic energy plus dissipation. The partition is set by loading period (viscous versus elastic limits) and viscosity structure. With a weak upper mantle, dissipation concentrates there except at long wavelengths and long periods, across periods of 7.63e-5 to 320 τM and wavelengths of 0.625D to 10D.

decisive_move.sentence: The systematic CitcomVE computation of 345 loading cases across viscosity structure, wavelength and period is what yields the partition, efficiency and spatial-distribution regularities.

gates.evidence: The parameter grid was chosen to sweep the space systematically, not directed by a stated hypothesis (p. 6). The numerical energy balance could have failed against the analytic relation (p. 7). The glacial estimate could have disagreed with Hanyk et al. and Huang et al. (p. 16). The regularities themselves face no test. Nothing is reported as fixed before the runs.

imports.item: Virtual work principle and Green's first identity for the energy balance
Linear Maxwell viscoelastic rheology and Maxwell relaxation time
Tidal heating of Io, Europa and Enceladus as the analog for exogenic dissipation
Citcom finite element code originally built for thermal convection in viscous fluids

novelty_claims.quote: these previous studies mainly estimated dissipative heating during specific processes, and did not explore systematically
Furthermore, these previous studies did not examine the energetics (i.e., energy balance and exchange) in the loading system.
[...] also shows that for long-wavelength loading at relatively long periods
we believe that this study represents an important step in understanding the dynamics of dissipative heating in planetary bodies

limits: No review file was supplied (the reviewers are only acknowledged, p. 18), so no review sequence is coded. composition is none_fits: the walk is a forward parametric simulation sweep with no rivals and no observations, so it is neither a trace series nor capability-first; exploration_first is the nearest, but a question was posed first. Sub-claims at other statuses: the Earth applications (about 3 mW/m2 for 100 kyr glacial cycles, about 9 mW/m2 for 40 kyr cycles, about 26-30 TW tidal heating at 4 Ga) are estimate_with_resolution in form, but no uncertainty or resolution is given; they are scalings from the 2-D Cartesian results. The weak-layer feedback (p. 17) is a hypothesis only. Only one viscosity contrast (a factor of 30) was tested, so the dependence on contrast magnitude is open (p. 14). The tidal estimate uses surface-only forcing with an ad hoc doubling for core-mantle boundary loading, and the 4 Ga lunar distance is taken from Qin et al. (2018). The authors list 2-D Cartesian geometry, uniform shear modulus and Maxwell rheology as limits (p. 18). No numerical convergence or resolution test is reported beyond the stated element sizes and time steps (inference from Table 2 and p. 6).

disagreements.support: The paper argues that earlier work estimated specific processes without a systematic parameter study or energy-balance analysis, and provides both.

alternatives_considered.alternatives: More sophisticated rheology models (e.g., Huang et al., 2018); variable shear modulus
